Playmaker exam book

The exam boards for step 12, one page each: the 17 exam boards, two candidate boards from the playtests, and two trainer tests that Contest as an action changed. Mark each page keep, fix (with a note) or drop.

How to read the pages
  • The court is the printed board: the rim is at the bottom, columns A to Q run left to right, rows 1 to 14 run up from the baseline. Left and right mean left and right as you look at the picture. The faint squares around the rim are the distance rings.
  • O1 to O5 are the offence (black circles). The player with the ball has a double circle and the ball.
  • X1 to X5 are the defence (red crosses). The small arrowhead on each X shows which way he faces.
  • A small M or Q tag under a player means he has used his Move or Quick Step this phase. LOCK marks a locked player.
  • Arrows drawn on the court show the move or pass the page is about, numbered in order.
  • Today's result is the All-Star in the step 6 run, on the clock with its full time, under the 9 November rules: Contest is an action (D-18), a turnover never scores more than the total banked before it (D-82), and every steal foul is +5 (D-89). These three apply to every board. The step 7 change (a steal foul on a shooter gives free throws only) came after that run; step 7 re-ran only the three marked tests (board 6 and the two trainer tests).
  • Four moves ahead means the All-Star searching a fixed four moves ahead with no time limit. That run was before 9 November, so today it is "not measured under the current rules". Its result before is given.
  • Phone speed is the run before 9 November at a quarter of the time budget, for all three levels.

Exam board 1

Straight laneFail

The situation
Five-out. O1 has the ball at the top of the key, just inside the arc. X1 trails behind him, two squares to his right and three back, so the straight line to the rim is open: before the defence acts, the drive is worth 32 against 22 for the offence's best other option. The defence is about to act.
What the computer should do
The defence takes away the straight drive: X1 recovers in front of O1, or a helper steps into the lane, or the drive is left open only if it is worse than what the offence already has.
The basketball reason
A ball handler with a straight line to the rim is the first thing a defence has to take away.
How it is judged
After the defence's turn, look at every move O1 could make straight toward the rim. The board is met if there is none, or if the best of them is worth less than the offence's best other option.

Exam board 2

Sag by shootingPass

The situation
Two copies of one board. O1 has the ball at the top, X2 guards O2 on the left wing. The only difference: on board A, O2 is a poor three-point shooter (rated 4); on board B, a good one (rated 12). The defence is about to act.
What the computer should do
X2 sags further off the poor shooter to help inside, and stays close enough to contest the good shooter.
The basketball reason
You give a poor shooter room and use the spare defender to protect the paint; you never leave a good shooter open.
How it is judged
After the defence's turn, X2 must be closer to the rim on board A than on board B, and on board B he must still be able to reach O2 to contest his shot.

Exam board 3

Help the helperFail

The situation
O1 has driven past X1 and has the ball in the lane, 3 squares from the rim. X1 is behind him and has used both his Move and his Quick Step, so he can't get back. O4 waits on the left baseline, guarded by X4 under the basket. The defence is about to act.
What the computer should do
A low defender steps up to stop O1, and another defender rotates to cover the man he left.
The basketball reason
When the ball handler beats his man, the nearest help has to stop the ball, and the next defender covers the open man so the kick-out isn't free.
How it is judged
After the defence's turn, at least one defender who was not next to O1 must end next to him, and at least one other defender must move.

Exam board 4

Two jobs, one defenderPass

The situation
O1 has the ball at the top of the key, inside the arc, with X1 behind him. O5 stands on the right block. X5 sits between them, off the passing line, so the pass to O5 can be thrown: it arrives half the time (X5 can step into it). The offence is about to act.
What the computer should do
The offence attacks X5: O1 shoots or drives, or passes to O5, and makes X5 choose.
The basketball reason
When one defender has two jobs, you attack him: whichever he picks, the other is open.
How it is judged
The offence's turn attacks X5: a shot, a pass to O5, or O1 moving or dribbling. It is also met if the computer picks a turn its own search rates above every attacking turn it weighs.

Exam board 5

CloseoutFail

The situation
O2 has just caught the ball on the left wing. X2 has closed out from 3 squares away, using his Move and his Quick Step. On board A he arrives next to O2; on board B he stops two squares short. The offence is about to act.
What the computer should do
Board A: O2 drives at the closeout, ending closer to the rim. Board B: O2 shoots now, or steps to a spot where no defender can reach him to Contest.
The basketball reason
Drive past a defender who arrives on a closeout; against one who stops short, take the open look, here or one step away.
How it is judged
Board A: O2 moves or dribbles, ends closer to the rim, and his first action is not a shot. Board B: his first action is a shot, or he moves to a square where no defender can Contest him.

Exam board 6 · D-111

Catch windowFail

The situation
O4 has just caught the ball in the left corner. Every defender is far from him: the nearest, X4, is in the lane and X2 is up at the top of the left side. The offence is about to act.
What the computer should do
O4 acts at once: he shoots the open corner three or attacks before the defence recovers.
The basketball reason
The moment after the catch, before the closeout arrives, is the best look the possession will get.
How it is judged
Judged by D-94: O4's open look (33) beats what the possession is worth now (24.9), so his first action must be his own: a shot, a movement or a dribble.
